title: Classes and objects
lesson:
In Level 1 you kept data in variables, lists and dictionaries, and wrote functions that work on that data. That works, until the data and the functions drift apart. A tank is a dict over here, `fill_tank(tank, litres)` is a function over there, and nothing stops some other line from doing `tank["level"] = -50`. A **class** bundles the data and the functions that belong to it into one thing.

A class is a blueprint. An **object** (also called an instance) is one real thing built from it. One `WaterTank` class, many tanks:

```
class WaterTank:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.level = 0

    def fill(self, litres):
        self.level = min(self.capacity, self.level + litres)

school = WaterTank(5000)
clinic = WaterTank(1000)
school.fill(800)
print(school.level, clinic.level)   # 800 0
```

- `__init__` runs when you make an object: `WaterTank(5000)`. It sets the starting state. It's called the **constructor**.
- `self` is the object the method is working on right now. Python passes it for you: `school.fill(800)` really means `WaterTank.fill(school, 800)`.
- `self.level` is an **attribute**: a variable that lives inside one object. Each tank has its own level.
- A **method** is a function written inside the class. It can read and change `self`.

Why bother? The rule "never above capacity" now lives in one place, inside `fill`. Every tank in the program follows it, and when the rule changes you change one method.

**Common mistakes**
- Forgetting `self` as the first parameter: `def fill(litres):`. Calling `tank.fill(10)` then fails with "takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given".
- Writing `level = 0` in `__init__` instead of `self.level = 0`. That makes a local variable that vanishes when `__init__` ends.
- Putting a list or dict directly under `class` (not inside `__init__`). That one list is **shared by every object**: add a member to one savings group and it shows up in all of them. Make lists and dicts inside `__init__`.

**In real programs** almost everything is an object. In a game, every enemy, bullet and chest is an object with its own health or position, and the game loop calls `enemy.update()` on each one. In robotics, a `Motor` object remembers its pin and speed. Class names use CapitalWords (`WaterTank`), methods and attributes use lower_case.

example.code:
class WaterTank:
    """A tank that knows its size and how full it is."""

    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.level = 0

    def fill(self, litres):
        space = self.capacity - self.level
        added = min(litres, space)
        self.level += added
        return added

    def percent(self):
        return self.level / self.capacity * 100


school = WaterTank(5000)
clinic = WaterTank(1000)
print(school.fill(800), clinic.fill(1500))
print(school.level, clinic.level)
print(f"clinic tank is {clinic.percent():.0f}% full")
notes: The class is the blueprint; the docstring says what one object is.
__init__ sets each new tank's starting state on self.
fill works out how much really fits, changes self.level and reports it.
Two objects, two separate levels: filling one doesn't touch the other.
clinic.fill(1500) only adds 1000 because the rule lives inside the method.

exercises.title: A water tank
exercises.prompt:
Finish the class WaterTank(capacity).
- __init__ stores capacity in self.capacity and starts self.level at 0.
- fill(litres): adds water but never above capacity. Returns the litres actually added.
- use(litres): takes water out but never below 0. Returns the litres actually given out.
- percent(): how full it is, level / capacity * 100.

tests.check:
t = WaterTank(500)
assert t.capacity == 500, 'capacity should be 500'
assert t.level == 0, 'a new tank starts at level 0'
tests.name: a new tank

tests.check:
t = WaterTank(500)
assert t.fill(200) == 200, 'fill(200) should return 200'
assert t.level == 200
assert t.use(50) == 50, 'use(50) should return 50'
assert t.level == 150, 'level should be 150, got %r' % t.level
tests.name: fill then use

tests.check:
t = WaterTank(1000)
t.fill(250)
assert t.percent() == 25, 'percent() should be 25, got %r' % t.percent()
tests.name: percent

tests.check:
t = WaterTank(100)
t.fill(80)
got = t.fill(50)
assert got == 20, 'only 20 more fits, so fill should return 20, got %r' % got
assert t.level == 100, 'level should stop at capacity'
tests.name: no overflow
tests.hint_if_fail: Work out the space left (capacity - level) and add whichever is smaller.

tests.check:
t = WaterTank(100)
t.fill(30)
got = t.use(50)
assert got == 30, 'only 30 is there, so use should return 30, got %r' % got
assert t.level == 0, 'level should stop at 0, got %r' % t.level
tests.name: can't go below empty

tests.check:
a = WaterTank(100)
b = WaterTank(100)
a.fill(60)
assert b.level == 0, 'filling one tank changed another one'
tests.name: each tank is separate

hints: Everything the object remembers goes on self: self.capacity = capacity, self.level = 0.
In fill, the space left is self.capacity - self.level. Add min(litres, space).
use is the mirror: given = min(litres, self.level), then self.level -= given and return given.

exercises.title: Player health
exercises.prompt:
Write a class Player(name, max_hp=100).
- Attributes: name, max_hp, and hp (starts equal to max_hp).
- take_damage(amount): hp goes down by amount but never below 0. A negative amount raises ValueError.
- heal(amount): hp goes up but never above max_hp.
- is_alive(): True while hp is above 0.

tests.check:
p = Player('Juma')
assert p.name == 'Juma' and p.max_hp == 100 and p.hp == 100, 'a new Player should have hp == max_hp == 100'
q = Player('Amina', 60)
assert q.hp == 60
tests.name: new players

tests.check:
p = Player('Juma')
p.take_damage(30)
assert p.hp == 70, 'hp should be 70, got %r' % p.hp
p.heal(10)
assert p.hp == 80
assert p.is_alive() is True
tests.name: damage and heal

tests.check:
p = Player('Juma', 50)
p.take_damage(80)
assert p.hp == 0, 'hp should stop at 0, got %r' % p.hp
assert p.is_alive() is False
tests.name: knocked out

tests.check:
p = Player('Juma', 50)
p.take_damage(5)
p.heal(100)
assert p.hp == 50, 'heal should stop at max_hp, got %r' % p.hp
tests.name: can't overheal

tests.check:
p = Player('Juma')
try:
    p.take_damage(-10)
    raise AssertionError('take_damage(-10) should raise ValueError (it would secretly heal)')
except ValueError:
    pass
assert p.hp == 100
tests.name: negative damage

hints: __init__ needs self.max_hp = max_hp and self.hp = max_hp.
max(0, ...) keeps a number from going below 0; min(self.max_hp, ...) keeps it from going above.
Check amount < 0 first and raise ValueError("...") before changing hp.

exercises.title: A savings group
exercises.prompt:
Write a class SavingsGroup(name) for a chama (a savings group).
- self.name, and self.members: a dict of member name -> balance, empty at the start.
- add_member(person): adds them with balance 0. Adding someone already in the group raises ValueError.
- deposit(person, amount): adds to their balance. Unknown person or amount <= 0 raises ValueError.
- balance(person): their balance. total(): everyone's money added up.

tests.check:
g = SavingsGroup('Umoja')
assert g.name == 'Umoja' and g.members == {}, 'a new group has no members'
g.add_member('Amina')
assert g.members == {'Amina': 0}, g.members
tests.name: add a member

tests.check:
g = SavingsGroup('Umoja')
for p in ['Amina', 'Juma']:
    g.add_member(p)
g.deposit('Amina', 500)
g.deposit('Juma', 200)
g.deposit('Amina', 100)
assert g.balance('Amina') == 600, g.balance('Amina')
assert g.total() == 800, g.total()
tests.name: deposits and total
refuses bad deposits

tests.check:
g = SavingsGroup('Umoja')
g.add_member('Amina')
g.deposit('Amina', 300)
try:
    g.add_member('Amina')
    raise AssertionError('adding Amina twice should raise ValueError')
except ValueError:
    pass
assert g.balance('Amina') == 300, 'adding her again must not reset her balance'
tests.name: no duplicates

tests.check:
a = SavingsGroup('Umoja')
b = SavingsGroup('Tumaini')
a.add_member('Juma')
assert b.members == {}, 'a member added to one group showed up in another: make the dict inside __init__, not under class'
tests.name: groups don't share members

hints: self.members = {} goes inside __init__, so each group gets its own dictionary.
Check the bad cases first (person in self.members, amount <= 0) and raise ValueError, then change the balance.

quiz.q: What is self inside a method?
choices: The object the method was called on
quiz.why: tank.fill(10) passes tank in as self.

quiz.q: a = WaterTank(100); b = WaterTank(100); a.fill(50). What is b.level?
quiz.why: Each object has its own attributes.

quiz.q: You wrote def fill(litres): inside the class and call tank.fill(10). What happens?
choices: TypeError: takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given
quiz.why: Python passes the object as the first argument, so self is missing.

quiz.q: Why does `members = []` written directly under `class Group:` cause trouble?
choices: Every Group object shares that one list
quiz.why: Class-level values are shared; make per-object lists in __init__ with self.

quiz.q: What is the main reason to use a class instead of a dict plus loose functions?
choices: The data and the rules that keep it valid live together
quiz.why: Bundling data with its behaviour keeps rules in one place.

cards.a: Sets up a new object's starting attributes when you call the class.
An attribute is data on the object (self.level); a method is a function in the class (fill).

cards.q: Where do you create a list each object needs?

explain: Explain the difference between a class and an object in your own words, using an example from a game or a farm that you make up.
